title: Graphs
html:
Graphs

Nodes and edges, and almost every relationship problem is one. The hard part is rarely the algorithm - it is recognising the graph, and choosing the representation.

Representation

Adjacency list - each node keeps its neighbours. O(V + E) space. The default: real graphs are sparse.

Adjacency matrix - a V×V grid. O(V²) space regardless of edges, but O(1) to ask "is there an edge". Worth it for dense graphs or when that question is the hot path.

Implicit - no structure at all. A grid where neighbours are the four adjacent cells; a set of states where edges are legal moves. Most real problems are this, and seeing it is the skill: "shortest sequence of moves" is a shortest path over states you never materialise.

Traversal

Depth-first - recursion or a stack. Cycle detection, connected components, topological order, flood fill.

Breadth-first - a queue. Finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph, because it reaches every node in order of edge count. This guarantee is the reason to use it, and it evaporates the moment edges have weights.

Both are O(V + E) and both need a visited set. Without one, a cycle means non-termination; on a grid, revisiting is also how an O(V+E) walk becomes exponential.

Shortest paths

Situation Algorithm Cost
Unweighted BFS O(V + E)
Non-negative weights Dijkstra O((V + E) log V) with a heap
Negative weights Bellman-Ford O(V × E)
All pairs, small V Floyd-Warshall O(V³)

Dijkstra is BFS with a priority queue instead of a queue - always expand the cheapest known node. It breaks with negative edges, because a node settled as final can later be improved. Bellman-Ford tolerates them and detects negative cycles, at a price.

Topological order

A linear order of a directed acyclic graph where every edge points forward. Build order, task scheduling, dependency resolution.

Two ways: DFS with post-order, reversed; or Kahn's algorithm, repeatedly taking nodes of in-degree zero. Kahn's has the nicer property that if it cannot place every node, the remainder is a cycle - so it detects the impossible case rather than producing nonsense.

Cycle detection differs by direction

  • Undirected: seeing a visited node that is not your parent means a cycle.
  • Directed: it must be a node on the current path, not merely visited before. Three colours - unvisited, in progress, done - or a recursion-stack set. Using plain "visited" reports cycles that do not exist.

Union-find

Near-O(1) "are these connected" and "merge these", with path compression and union by rank. The right tool for connectivity as edges arrive, for Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, and for counting components without a traversal. Note what it cannot do: it tracks connectivity, not paths.

Common mistakes

  • No visited set, or marking visited at the wrong moment - mark on enqueue, not on dequeue, or nodes enter twice.
  • BFS on a weighted graph.
  • Dijkstra with negative weights.
  • Treating an undirected edge as one directed edge; it is two.
  • Recursive DFS on a large graph, overflowing the stack where an explicit stack would not.
